summary: Return all distinct subsets of a list that may contain duplicates.
mainInsight: Sort first so equal values are adjacent. When enumerating, a subset that uses a duplicate value without using its immediately preceding equal value is a repeat of one already produced - skip it.

approaches.name: Generate all and de-duplicate with a set
Backtracking with sibling skipping
approaches.summary: Skip nums[i] when i > start and nums[i] == nums[i - 1].

approaches.name: Bitmask + duplicate rule
approaches.summary: Reject masks that take nums[i] without nums[i-1] when equal.
weaknesses: Enumerates all 2^n masks even if many are skipped

personalSolution.approach: Bitmask enumeration with a duplicate-skip rule
personalSolution.notes: Correct. The backtracking version avoids enumerating the rejected masks.

promptVariants: What is the rule that removes duplicate subsets after sorting?
When is taking nums[i] a duplicate?
options: Taking nums[i] equal to nums[i-1] without taking nums[i-1]
Taking any element twice in the same subset
Taking the largest element before all the others
Taking an empty subset at every recursion level
cards.answer: Taking nums[i] equal to nums[i-1] without taking nums[i-1]
cards.explanation: The copies are interchangeable, so one canonical choice is to take them from the left: use the second copy only if the first is used.

incorrectOptionExplanations.Taking any element twice in the same sub: Elements are used at most once.

promptVariants: Why does the rule 'use the second copy only if the first is used' remove duplicates exactly?
How does this relate to `i > start` in the backtracking version?
cards.answer: For k equal copies a subset with j of them can be formed in many ways; requiring the used copies to be the leftmost j makes each multiset appear once. In the backtracking version `i > start and nums[i] == nums[i-1]` skips choosing a later copy as a sibling at the same level, which enforces the same canonical choice.
cards.explanation: Sort first or equal values are not adjacent.

cards.answer: O(n) for the current subset and loop variables; no recursion.
cards.explanation: Backtracking needs O(n) recursion depth too.

promptVariants: Explain the skip condition `i > 0 and nums[i] == nums[i-1] and not (mask & (1 << (i-1)))`.
cards.answer: If nums[i] equals the previous value but the previous element is NOT in the mask, this subset uses the second copy without the first, which duplicates the subset that uses the first copy instead - so the whole mask is rejected. Sorting makes equal values adjacent so that 'previous element' is the previous copy.
keyPoints: Same value, previous copy unused => duplicate
cards.explanation: Backtracking avoids even generating those masks.

promptVariants: How many distinct subsets does [3,3,3] have?
cards.explanation: [], [3], [3,3], [3,3,3]; 8 would count the same subset several times.

incorrectOptionExplanations.8: 8 = 2^3 counts equal subsets of different positions separately.
incorrectOptionExplanations.7: 7 would count [3] and [3,3] more than once.
